analysis.one_liner: Requires private and state prisons holding federal detainees to disclose records under FOIA.
analysis.headline: The Private Prison Information Act of 2023 was introduced with 13 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says that records held by private prisons, state prisons, and local jails that house federal prisoners under contract with the government must be treated like federal records under the Freedom of Information Act, the law that lets the public request government documents. A federal agency could only withhold such records if it can point to a specific harm that fits a FOIA exemption, or if another law forbids release. Contractors would have to keep records in searchable formats and include compliance as a required term of their contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people — detainees' families, journalists, watchdog groups, and researchers — gain the right to request records about conditions, staffing, deaths, and complaints at privately run and state or local facilities holding federal prisoners, information currently outside FOIA's reach.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes any record related to a nonfederal prison, correctional, or detention facility holding federal prisoners or detainees a federal agency record subject to FOIA, closing a gap that lets private and state or local facilities escape federal open-records rules.

It covers both privately owned or operated facilities and state or local jails that hold federal detainees under contract with a federal agency, so the rule applies across the network of contract detention.

A federal agency could not withhold covered records unless it independently foresees a specific identifiable harm protected by a FOIA exemption, or disclosure is prohibited by law — a stricter standard than blanket secrecy.
Contractors must keep records in readily reproducible, searchable formats, and within one year agencies must add compliance as a required term of existing contracts.

analysis.who_pays: Private prison companies and state or local jails holding federal detainees bear the cost of building the record systems and answering public records requests; the cost to taxpayers is minimal.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison companies and local jails

drawbacks.text: The bill applies FOIA obligations to state and local jails that house federal detainees, not just private companies, which imposes administrative and record-keeping costs on local governments that had no say in the federal contract.

Transparency would not be absolute: agencies could still withhold records under existing FOIA exemptions (such as security and law-enforcement exemptions), so the bill narrows secrecy rather than eliminating it.
New compliance obligations for contractors could feed into contract pricing, adding some public cost to the oversight benefit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are real but modest: record systems and request-handling at facilities that already operate with public money. The benefit — public access to information about deaths, medical care, and conditions in places holding federal detainees — addresses a genuine accountability gap. The design is straightforward and narrowly targeted at federally contracted detention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, with 10 original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, its only action; no further steps appear in the record for the rest of the Congress.
Thirteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
The bill received no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so it did not become law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison operators and the state and local jails that hold federal detainees came out ahead: they keep operating without any federal open-records obligation. The public lost a transparency tool, and the 13 cosponsors gained nothing for it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison operators and contract jails

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 14, 2023, and never scheduled a markup, hearing, or vote on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 cosponsors were House Democrats, no Republicans sponsored or cosponsored it, and the Republican-run Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Companies like CoreCivic and GEO Group hold federal contracts to detain prisoners and immigrants; the bill would subject their records on conditions, deaths, and staffing to FOIA requests for the first time. Their interest in keeping operations opaque runs against the public's interest in oversight of publicly funded detention.

industries.industry: State and local jails housing federal detainees
industries.note: These facilities receive federal funds to hold federal prisoners and would face new obligations to produce searchable records and answer FOIA requests. Their interest in limiting disclosure of jail conditions runs against the public's transparency interest, though the bill does not reduce their funding.
